paras: The Wynn "possum hunter" whippings were a night raid in mid-August 1915 in which fifteen masked, armed men went to the homes of white and Black residents near Wynn, in northern Christian County, Kentucky, whipped several people, and left notices ordering them out of the community. One white man and one Black woman were known to have been whipped, and two white men who had been warned left the area. Papers outside Kentucky ran the story as a revival of night riding in western Kentucky, and one dispatch warned of a "race war."

The raid was reported together with night-rider activity in neighboring Caldwell County, where a warning note and a bundle of thorn switches were left at the Princeton brickyard of J. K. McGoodwin. That notice, signed "Possum Hunters," told McGoodwin to get rid of his Black workers and to "save your neck," and he dismissed them at once.

According to news that reached Hopkinsville, the band struck "a few nights" before the first reports of 19 August, near the place called Wynns or Wynn post office. Fifteen men, masked and armed, went to a number of houses belonging to both white and Black residents. A white man and a Black woman were whipped, and the lash was reportedly applied to ten others. At most of the houses the raiders left notices telling the occupants to move out of the community.

Two white men who had been warned left, and an exodus of Black residents was expected. Across the two counties, the Lexington dispatch said, some Black residents were leaving for safer counties or for Indiana, while others had armed themselves and refused to be driven out because they owned their homes. The same dispatch noted that state authorities had taken no action, and no arrests of the Wynn raiders appear in the coverage.

The first national report was a Nashville wire built on "specials" from Princeton and Hopkinsville, which the Washington Evening Star headed "'Possum Hunters' Feared" on 19 August. Over the next three days the Newark Evening Star, the Harrisburg Telegraph and the Richmond Virginian printed the same text under headlines about night riders becoming active again. The wire named no victims and gave no motive, coupling the Christian County whippings with the threat against McGoodwin's Black laborers.

A separate Lexington dispatch in the East St. Louis Daily Journal took a sharper line under the headline "Kentucky Race War Feared." It described the raids as "outrages," said the Wynn victims were "beaten almost to death," and blamed the trouble on Black workers employed "where white men formerly were." The Hartford Herald, printing a Hopkinsville report on 25 August under "Regulators Whip White Man and Negro Woman," instead passed on word that the band was trying "to regulate the morals" of the neighborhood. All of these reports ran in white papers; no Black-press account of the Wynn raid was found.

The reports differ on how badly the victims were hurt: the Hopkinsville report says only that they were whipped, while the Lexington dispatch says they were beaten almost to death. They also differ on motive, with the Hopkinsville report pointing to the policing of local morals and the Lexington dispatch to a campaign against Black labor, backed by an order that every Black person at Wynn leave "on pain of death." The Hopkinsville account came from telephone messages from the neighborhood, while the Lexington dispatch covered both counties and is the only source for the death threat.

reader.title: Wynn "possum hunter" whippings
bases: A masked, armed band calling itself 'possum hunters' or 'night riders' went to houses at night, whipped residents, and left notices ordering them out of the community (A1, A4, A8).

Three separately sourced reports agree on a masked band whipping a white man and a Black woman near Wynn and leaving notices to move: the Nashville wire (A1), a Lexington dispatch (A4), and a Hopkinsville report (A8).

accounts.label: Nashville wire (specials from Princeton and Hopkinsville)
accounts.gist: Fifteen masked, armed men went to homes of white and Black people in northern Christian County; several were whipped and notices to move were left.

accounts.label: Lexington dispatch
accounts.gist: Night riders in Christian and Caldwell counties threatened a 'race war'; at Wynn post office a white man and a Black woman were beaten almost to death and every Black resident was ordered out on pain of death; the trouble was blamed on Black workers replacing white men.

accounts.label: Hopkinsville report (telephone messages)
accounts.gist: A band of 'possum hunters' near Wynns whipped one white man and one Black woman and reportedly ten others, left notices at most houses, and was believed to be trying to regulate the neighborhood's morals.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed the wire '"POSSUM HUNTERS" FEARED. Masked and Armed Men Terrorizing Two Kentucky Counties.'
Newark, Harrisburg and Richmond papers ran the same wire under 'Night Riders in Kentucky', 'Kentucky Night Riders Out' and 'Night Riders Again Busy in Kentucky'.
The East St. Louis Daily Journal headlined 'KENTUCKY RACE WAR FEARED', called the raids 'outrages', and attributed them to Black workers taking jobs white men had held.
The Hartford Herald headlined 'REGULATORS WHIP WHITE MAN AND NEGRO WOMAN' and passed on the belief that the band was regulating local morals.
